The Yellow River, or Huang He. The second-longest river in Asia and historically the most dangerous, flowing approximately fifty-four hundred sixty-four kilometers from the Tibetan Plateau eastward across northern China to the Bohai Sea. Its distinctive yellow color, caused by loess sediment transported from the plateau, gave it its name and made it a symbol of Chinese civilization, though its catastrophic floods earned it the darker name of China's Sorrow.

The Yellow River flows from the high Tibetan Plateau across the Loess Plateau, picking up fine silt that gives it its yellowish hue. It is responsible for some of history's deadliest floods. The nineteen thirty-one inundation killed an estimated one to four million people. The Grand Canal, built in the seventh century, connected the Yellow River to the Yangtze, enabling grain transport to the capital and representing a major feat of engineering.

Major cities include Xi'an, Luoyang, and Kaifeng, ancient centers of Chinese imperial power and culture. The river's unpredictable course shifts forced the ancient capital to move multiple times as the river changed channel across the North China Plain. Dike construction and maintenance was a defining feature of Chinese governance and engineering for over two thousand years. In modern times, water scarcity threatens the region. The river now often runs dry before reaching the sea, endangering agriculture and cities that depend on its flow.
